utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, please continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: One more time, I would like to advise you and request of you, because of all these technical matters, that we have to really focus on the questions, which will be brief, so that we can finish as quickly as we can. And I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, would you please turn off your mike after your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, you were brought to the military investigative judges in Mostar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who it was, whether that was an investigator or magistrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: A prosecutor was present, as well as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm not asking about an impression; but as a citizen of Mostar, did you recognise the court building in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the court building, that was the faculty building. Not the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: At that time, the court was moved to the faculty building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: As president of the Crisis Staff regarding the -- at the request of the Crisis Staff, it had been moved to that building after the aggression of the Serbs in '92?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The judge read you a decision about your detention and the provisional detention of 30 days?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that I was taken from the Heliodrom from there, and I never -- and I was never brought back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But you were handed in a decision on a provisional detention of 30 days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When were you in the military investigative prison in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: A month after I had been brought to Heliodrom, I was taken to Ljubuski. So I don't know exactly when it was because there were some Croats there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Croats were there, too?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, they were there, too. But because they were all civilians, the educated persons, I did not gain an impression that this was an investigative prison; that is, it looked more like a camp to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All these Croats and the intellectuals that you mentioned, they all had similar decisions of the investigative judge handed to them?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell me, after you were released from this investigative prison, you were placed in the public security station in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was taken straight to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Perhaps you did not understand me. Well, I was referring to the point after Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, after Ljubuski, I went straight to Heliodrom. After Heliodrom, from the Heliodrom, under the auspices of the Red Cross, I was exchanged at Kocine. I never saw the MUP building again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you given a document at the exchange, the record of the exchange?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you aware that at that time, people who were under investigation, if they were exchanged, the investigation could have been suspended and the suspect could have been exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I was not aware that I was a suspect or that there would be an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The investigator in charge read you the reasons why criminal proceedings had been launched against you, which is provided for in the law books in Herzegovina and the procedure for launching of criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I never saw the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But as an educated man, you were aware that you were in court and in front of a judge?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no such feeling that he was a judge and that that was a court. Here I feel like I'm before a Court and before serious people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you feel like that only before this Court or any other court?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never -- I have never been in front of a court until today, so I have no particular feeling, how it looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you recognise Croatian courts?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time it could not have been a Croatian court. The Croatian State is something completely different. It could have been some kind of Municipal Court of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you recognise the courts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I would have recognised such a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: At that time, the Military Court was the Military Court of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Crisis Staff, and I did not have such information because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Can you please tell me, when did you arrive at the Public Security Station?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th, around 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: October, which year, which date?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was '93. Of course, the conflict started on the 9th, and on the 10th we were all led out of the building where we lived and taken to the SUP, so it was on the 10th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the police station, that is, the Public Security Station, you were processed, and then, along with a criminal report, you were remanded to the investigative judge to make a decision about your further detention, based on the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the Public Security Station, you had your own office, with a TV set in it, you had your room where you slept and an office where you received friends and associates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to mention a name which may clue somebody in to the identity of this witness. So for just that one question, could we please move into the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, this meeting, you said, was also attended by Mrs. Bisera Turkovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the ambassador in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. Can you tell me, the delegation of HZ H-B I think at that time was already -- were they distributing some documents to the representatives of the International Community?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You attended the meeting throughout?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You sat all at the same table?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all in a coffee bar that was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And in front of you, nobody distributed any documents to the representatives of the International Community?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please -- you told my learned friend of the Prosecution that Professor Hadziosmanovic was relieved of his duty towards the end of '92; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Not relieved of his duty, but simply he was -- he had two positions and then he continued in just one position, and I was appointed to that second position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That is fine. I'm just verifying that because of one fact. Now, tell me, President Izetbegovic, the president of your party, was in Mostar on several occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it was several times. I think it was twice. Very early on, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you know that he once spent a night at Mr. Hadziosmanovic's and the second time at Mr. Karabeg's?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: On the second occasion when he stayed with Mr. Karabeg, you were present with him all the time, and what followed that visit was the removal of Mr. Hadziosmanovic from his post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to refer to the document that was provided by the Prosecution, and the witness does not have the document in front of him. Can he please be provided the Exhibit 218, 219, from yesterday's session, the document that was put to him by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could I remind you that those documents were temporarily put under seal by the Prosecution, so you should bear in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I am taking that into account. I have one question regarding the document. I'm actually not going to discuss the contents of the documents but just verify a signature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So will you please open the Croatian version of that document. On page 2, there is some stamps and some signatures. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krsnik, my apology again. I think at least one of these documents was identified. And for the same reasons as before, if we are going to do this, unfortunately we have to go back into private session, because if he says...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay, we will go back to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the upper left corner -- may I proceed, Your Honours? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the upper left corner, is that the emblem of your party, the SDA?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me -- would you please be so kind and turn the page? Is this the seal of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be something local, some improvisation. It's much more robust.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What do you mean, "local"?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it looks rather puny to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You see, this document, above that seal we see that the document comes from Sarajevo, and that is the SDA secretary, the secretary of the SDA, as such?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you if you saw it before. I'm asking you if you can identify it, the seal.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I repeat that something -- I can't recognise -- I do not see it, I cannot -- I do not see it as the proper emblem of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But have you heard of the SDA secretary, Mr. Cengic?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just answered that a while ago. Until November, I didn't know any one of them. And even after November, I didn't know too many, apart from my region, because I had no communication with Sarajevo so I was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the permission of the Chamber, may I read some passages from this document and ask the witness if he can tell us something about that, as a high SDA official? It has to be translated to him. If the document is going to be read, could these parts of the document be placed on the ELMO, please, because the interpreters do not have copies of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we have the English translation. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course. This is the translation of this document in Croatian, which I have it. If you do not think it is necessary, then I will not go into that. I only wanted to ask one question. But, right, I can ask a question even without reading the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You were conversant with the SDA policy, weren't you, and about the deliberate evacuation of Bosniaks so as to present them as victims to the rest of the world?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But since you were in Bugojno, do you know the fate of Croats in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But did you hear, at least afterwards, that they had all been expelled, ethnically cleansed, by Bosniaks in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: As a high-ranking SDA officer, did you know that they were ethnically cleansed, that is, expelled from Konjic and Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: During your missions, did you visit the camps with detained Croats prior to the conflict on the 9th of May in Mostar? Did you lend them any assistance, camps such as the museum at Jablanica with 1.000 Croats, mostly women and children, then Musala in Konjic, Celebic at Konjic, elementary school in Bijelo Polje, Mostar? Did you ever go there? This was all prior to the 9th of May, 1993. Did you have any information about them and did you go there?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you're really giving a very hard time to the interpreters and the typists. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So as a high-ranking SDA official, you had no idea that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell us, was the government of the Bosnian people taking place through the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the final thing of the arming needed to form the Muslim army, was it done through Islamic organisations throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that. I was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And never at the SDA meetings, you never talked about arming your army?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us, when you were taken into custody following the criminal report, after you were taken to the investigating judge, was a large amount of German marks found on you?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 100.000 German marks. The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did it cross Armija? Do you have any information about that? I mean the Croatian State.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know. It wasn't my business. My business was to try to bring the tensions down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not 100.000. The transcript says 1.000, and my question was whether when the witness was taken to the police station in Mostar for interview, were 100.000 German marks found on the gentleman. And his answer was "No." Am I right? The witness confirms, merely for the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: (redacted) Alija Vidimilic, Salih Cemalovic, and Edo Rizvanovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Perhaps I was there, perhaps I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you recall at that meeting discussing that Dajdza had provided a thousand rifles for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you tell the Chamber if you know who Dajdza is?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you hear that he was an officer in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he was a man -- an officer in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you heard that he was a Bosnian by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him as Mato Sarlija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mato Sarlija, Dajdza. And his real name, do you know his real name?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you present at a meeting of the regional board on the 16th of April, 1993 with Safet Orucevic, Efendi Tinjak, Efendi Kojic, Mito Hujdur, Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to repeat those names? I'm asking the interpreters. Should I repeat those last names? Perhaps I was too fast. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So which was attended by Mufti of Herzegovina, Efendi Kojic, Efendi Tinjak, Efendi Omerika, Safet Orucevic, Zijo Demirovic, Mito Hujdur. Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I was; maybe I wasn't. I don't remember. There were a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number of Bosniaks meeting to discuss individual issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me remind you it was a joint meeting of the Islamic community and all members of the Mostar SDA.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be. I mean, stood to reason to cooperate with all institutions working with the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you remember how Mithat Hujdur on that occasion said that in an hour's time, Mostar would be taken?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't that kind of man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. He would still be alive had he been that kind of man. And do you remember that on the same occasion, you -- and that was also the meeting when the schism between Muslims took place. Do you remember that you said on that occasion that Muslim interest in Mostar has only one mentor in the person of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and you said that Mostar needs to be a Muslim city in all its glory?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think I could think something like that even in a dream in view of my previous life there of 50 years. There's no way I could have said anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, the Vance-Owen Plan guaranteeing equal rights to all three ethnic communities, the SDA refused to sign that plan. But with the HDZ of Herzegovina, you nevertheless divided the territory into provinces pursuant to an agreement between Izetbegovic and Boban,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Scott is standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've tried to avoid interrupting but for some minutes now, we are going back and forth between identifying information. I have tried not to intervene. I think at this point we have to go into private session, perhaps stay there for a while because-- well, I'm not going to say anything more in open session. I think we must go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll have that in the transcript redacted accordingly. Now shall we go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, I am going to conduct the cross-examination on behalf of the other accused, and I think we can stay in the open session. May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness O. I am Mr. Zelimir Par. I am one of the co-counsels of the accused Vinko Martinovic. And let me ask you first about an event which you referred to today -- actually yesterday, which you said that it took place in April 1993, and this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par, would you please turn off your microphone after your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. However, I have not quite yet posed the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: This was the so-called attack against the SDA -- on the SDA premises carried out by the persons named Takac and Blazevic?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question to you is can you be more precise about the date in April when this took place, perhaps you recall the date or perhaps there is even a document in the SDA archives which registered that event?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident took place in April. I'm not sure that I would be able to give you the exact date. And as far as documents are concerned, I think that during the attack, all documents were destroyed in possession of the regional board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, regarding that same period, can you tell me whether at that time, Mostar was already a divided city? Was there a line of separation at Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe no -- not, because I lived on the west side, and a large number of citizens lived in the west side. And I don't think that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can we agree that it was only after 9th of May, after the attack, that this line was established, that the armed units were deployed there and that, de facto, the city was divided at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and that line of separation remained there until the end of war. And it can still be seen to date where the two sides were during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I would like to move on to another area of questioning. From your evidence, which you gave yesterday and today, I noticed that you actually testified in two ways; one was your personal suffering and the suffering of your family, which was sometimes tinged with emotion, which we all appreciated. However, you also gave a different kind of evidence regarding political assessment of the political circumstances in Mostar at the time. You talked about the aggression, about the plans of Croats. You talked not only about things that you personally experienced, but also about the future borders that Croats were contemplating, who said what, who had what intentions. And without going into any of the specifics of those issues, I'm trying to establish the position which you implicitly hold when giving such answers. So all these political judgements which you offered during your evidence yesterday and today, did you present them believing yourself to be an expert on those issues, and can you argue these contentions, or are these simply your thoughts based on your experience from the period, based on your political involvement in these affairs, or are these your personal views and opinions, if you can answer briefly?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: "Yes" means these are your personal views and conclusions?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, these personal views, opinions and conclusions that you just confirmed, did they coincide with the positions of the SDA party, of which you are a member?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they did, because I could not be a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: When you said you couldn't be that, does that mean that you feel yourself bound by the party discipline, as you put it to yourself today?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The platform that I adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just about five or six questions of clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness O, there were some questions about the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the time of that referendum, who was attacking, what nation or group of people was attacking the Croat and Bosniak communities?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs, that is, the JNA, with the paramilitary units of the State of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in declaring the sovereign independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was independence from whom?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was independence -- the transition led to that. It was the first time in history that Bosnia was able to declare itself for what it was. All the ethnic groups that were mentioned by the learned colleague yesterday, Slovenes, Croats, Serbs, Macedonians, Montenegrins all gained their own state, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was being liquidated as a state, it was supposed to disappear. But the United Nations recognised it after the referendum. And after the referendum, the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina was hoisted on the East River.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness O, thank you for your answer. But listen very specifically, please, to my question now, and that is: From what former country or nation - or collection of countries - was it that by this referendum the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina was declaring its sovereign independence? From whom, or what, if that's perhaps better?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Yugoslavia, which was composed of Serbia and Montenegro and, of course, of all other former republics which made up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what would have been the result, if you will, if the referendum had not been passed by both the Bosniak and Croatian people; what would the result have been?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The result would have been a division. Serbia wanted its part, Croatia wanted its own part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, turning to one other topic in about one question or two: The questions concerning Mr. Hadziosmanovic, if he was at some times out of step with the SDA platform, can you tell the Chamber, please, why he was not also removed as the head of the SDA in Mostar? Why was he left in that position?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was left in that position because it was a local position at the level of Mostar and only in the area where we lived, that is, half of Mostar, because the aggressor was on the other side. And it was expected -- it was perceived that he had gone astray and that things needed to be corrected, that he had -- and there was a platform which stated clearly that Bosnia and Herzegovina was a unified country consisting of three ethnic groups, and that all of the sides were constituent parts, and that the Bosniaks were a constituent part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Final question, then: Is it fair to say that the SDA essentially were exercising some discipline on Mr. Hadziosmanovic without, however, removing him from this second post?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it is clear, when somebody is holding two posts and one is taken away, it is a kind of a pressure on this person. But time showed that after the conflict, Mr. Hadziosmanovic embraced other options which were damaging to the Bosniak population, and had he sided with his own people, he wouldn't -- that would not have been the end of his career.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Clark has a question to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness O, this document that was given to you by Mr. Krsnik, is it a document -- do I understand your evidence to be that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you don't recognise the title of the party on the beginning of the document in Serbo-Croatian? Yes, that document.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it seems to me this was in handwriting. I had never seen it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. So your evidence is it doesn't look like the normal heading of a document emanating from the headquarters of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it doesn't. The only justification may be the wartime and just lack of resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. So your evidence is it isn't the normal appearance of a document, but it could be a document from the SDA?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: One should probably ask those who compiled it and who signed it. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we haven't heard where this document came from, but I'm sure in due course we will. But you don't recognise it as being in the usual format, and you can't say any more than that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say more than that. In fact, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge Clark's questions? No, it seems to me "no". Thank you, thank you, Witness. Thank you very much for coming to help us and to testify before this Trial Chamber. The usher will show you out of the room when he pulls down the blinds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With your permission, if I can make a brief comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, I would like to say that I am very excited by the way we were received, and I think that this is a very professional atmosphere. One feels very good and very safe in this environment, and I want to thank you one more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber would like to give our best wishes to you in the building of the beautiful town of Mostar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: During the course of the direct examination of this witness, the Prosecution proposed to tender certain documents; namely, P125.1, P126.1, P218, P219 and P480. This Trial Chamber would like to know the initial response from the Defence counsels' side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of the first accused, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, in respect of these four documents, does not object to their being put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Vinko Martinovic has no objections to the introduction of these exhibits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This Trial Chamber will make the decision in due time. Now is the time for a break. We will adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As you may have heard from the announcement, this Tribunal of the United Nations has requested all the United Nations Duty Stations to observe three minutes in silence to pay respect to those innocent lives who died in that terrible incident, at 12.00 sharp. We will be reminded at that time. As for the first set of documents we discussed before the break, this Trial Chamber believes that since there is no objections from the both sides, they are admitted into the evidence. And Registrars will be instructed with the proper number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: His Honour, this document submitted by the OTP will be admitted into evidence. So they are EP5, EP125.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we don't have to do it right now. Maybe we could do it next Monday, after full consultations with the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So I would be able to give all the numbers by then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there's something that I would like to say; that is, after the Trial Chamber has heard the two first Prosecution witnesses, it feels that it has to remind both parties of the time frame that was scheduled for this case. As indicated already at Pre-Trial stage of the proceedings, and reiterated by this Trial Chamber at the opening of the trial, both parties have ten weeks to present their cases to the Chamber. The Pre-Trial Judge, Judge Wald, told me that she has persuaded the Prosecution to reduce the number of witnesses to 50. If taking into account the ten weeks, every week we will have five witnesses, which means one witness for each day. At the conclusion of the first week of the Prosecution's case, the Trial Chamber is concerned to see that neither of the parties presents and cross-examines the witnesses in a way that is sufficiently efficient and concise to guarantee the expeditiousness of the trial. The Trial Chamber has the impression that proceedings seem to run considerably behind the schedule. For this reason, and in the full consideration of the rights of the accused, the Trial Chamber wishes to call upon the parties to strictly adhere to the following in furtherance of a fair and expedient trial while examining and cross-examining witnesses in the coming weeks: Questions should be put to the witnesses in a short and clear way. There's no need for counsel to give a lengthy introduction before actually putting his question to the witness. A short and direct question, which should generally not be leading, will help the witness to respond with likewise clear and a direct answer. The counsel asking the witness should direct the witness to the very issue and prevent him or her from deviating from the question. The Trial Chamber is fully aware and respects the fact the witnesses before the Trial Chamber are generally very anxious to give a full account of what happened to them during the conflict. However, the Trial Chamber has to insist that witnesses are asked by the questioning counsel to stick to their questions, not only for the reason of trial constraints but also because of the necessity that evidence is presented clearly linked to the complete indictment. The parties will inform their witnesses accordingly and explain that this is in the witness's very interest to provide the Trial Chamber with specific and clear evidence that relates directly to the charges of the case concerned, because only such evidence can be considered when making the findings. The Trial Chamber further elects to ask the parties to refer to the Chamber to the parts of the indictment that are being addressed in the course of the examination or cross-examination of a witness. This will help the Trial Chamber to follow the evidence presented closely, which again, is in the interest of both parties. The compliance of the parties with the aforementioned principles is indispensable to the conduct of these proceedings with due regard to the rights of the accused and in a reasonable time frame, and is therefore appreciated by the Trial Chamber. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to belabour these issues now, because we do have witnesses waiting and, of course, only a short remaining time for today's schedule. I would like to ask that the Chamber provide an opportunity at some point, perhaps when we don't have a witness facing quite such urgency, to address the matters a bit further. A very, very quick response, Your Honour, is this: We have certainly always anticipated that some of our witnesses would be longer than others. I think you will find before this trial is over that some of the witnesses will be quite short in time. However, it was clear that some witnesses, such especially as these first ones, and some others later, will be -- will take more time, will cover more of the issues in the case, more of a background, more of the political issues, if you will, and will take more time. So I must say it was always anticipated, for instance, that the second witness will take a substantial amount of time. And that's not, at least to us, was not a surprise. I must say, Your Honours, and again, I don't want to delay the next witness too much, we are frankly -- I must say we have been a bit surprised about this ten-week schedule and the mention of 50 witnesses. We are not aware of any prior ruling to that effect. There had been conversation -- there had been dialogue between counsel and the Pre-Trial Judge about these matters, but I can tell you that the Prosecution Bench was unaware of any past ruling about ten weeks and 50 witnesses. We will do our best to present the case as efficiently as we can, but I would be less than honest if I didn't tell the Chamber that these schedules come as news to us. But we will do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I would like to remind you of the list of the witnesses you provided to this Trial Chamber before the trial and every description of the facts of the testimony. There is estimated time for each witness. I just hope you adhere to this time schedule you proposed in your list. Yes, Mr. Krsnik. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My learned friend has already stated his view on the schedule of our work, and I thought that I should do it also on behalf of Mr. Naletilic. I wish to confirm and agree with what our learned friends say. We have never adopted any decision on the duration or the number of witnesses. So the Defence wishes to say it's surprised. If it is brought down to 50 witnesses, the Defence simply cannot provide proper defence with only 50 witnesses. It is really too few. But this is the first time we hear about this, so on this occasion we merely wanted to state our surprise with this new information. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, briefly, I confirm what our learned friends from the OTP have said and what my Colleague Krsnik has said. We are indeed taken by surprise by this, and I think we shall need your instructions in this regard so that we can comply with the decisions of the Chamber. And I should also like to ask that we try to reach somehow some agreement in this case, and I apologise for raising this matter. But so far the practice in this Tribunal was that the cross-examination could take, as we have two accused here, two clients, that that could take as much time as the direct examination, so half of the time should be accorded to Mr. Krsnik and half of the time should be used by me. Do we agree with this? Do you agree with this, at least that's how it will be in this case, that each one of us will be accorded half of the time allotted to the direct examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the equality of arms does not necessarily mean that you use exactly equal time for both parties. It depends on the contents of the questioning. This Trial Chamber will take note of the views expressed by both sides. So, Mr. Scott, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Stringer will be handling the next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning, and good morning to Your Honours. The next witness, Your Honour, is the subject of a specific decision which was issued by the former composition of Trial Chamber I, Judges Rodrigues, Riad and Wald, the decision dated 22nd of January, 2001, and it provides, first and foremost, that the proceedings in respect of this witness will take place in closed session. And I have a couple of brief introductory comments to make about the decision, but perhaps I should make those in closed session, and I would ask that we move into closed session at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 12.59 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of September, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
